blocks.es_reference: Unidad 10 · 2 Timoteo 2:15 · Los números de Strong en tres formas

blocks.en: Strong's Numbers — The Bridge to Every Hebrew and Greek Word
blocks.es_reference: Los números de Strong — El puente a toda palabra hebrea y griega

blocks.en: "Be diligent to present yourself approved to God, a worker who does not need to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth."
blocks.es_reference: «Procura con diligencia presentarte a Dios aprobado, como obrero que no tiene de qué avergonzarse, que traza bien la palabra de verdad».

blocks.en: Unit Scripture: "Be diligent to present yourself approved to God, a worker who does not need to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth." — 2 Timothy 2:15 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: Escritura de la Unidad: «Procura con diligencia presentarte a Dios aprobado, como obrero que no tiene de qué avergonzarse, que traza bien la palabra de verdad». — 2 Timoteo 2:15 (RVG)

blocks.en: Orientation: A Professor and Twenty-Seven Years
blocks.es_reference: Orientación: Un profesor y veintisiete años

blocks.en: In 1863, the year Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation and Lee invaded Pennsylvania, a forty-one-year-old Methodist professor of Hebrew and Greek at Drew Theological Seminary in New Jersey began a project so vast that his colleagues thought he had lost his senses. His name was James Strong. His project was to take every single word of the English King James Bible — every the, every and, every God, every love, every righteousness, every kyrios and every dikaiosynê — and trace it back to the exact Hebrew or Greek word behind it, then assign each Hebrew word and each Greek word a unique number that any English-only reader could use. He wanted to put the original languages in the hand of the plowboy.
blocks.es_reference: En 1863, el año en que Lincoln firmó la Proclamación de Emancipación y Lee invadió Pensilvania, un profesor metodista de hebreo y griego de cuarenta y un años en el Seminario Teológico Drew en Nueva Jersey comenzó un proyecto tan vasto que sus colegas pensaron que había perdido la razón. Su nombre era James Strong. Su proyecto era tomar cada palabra de la Biblia inglesa King James — cada el, cada y, cada Dios, cada amor, cada justicia, cada kyrios y cada dikaiosynê — y rastrearla hasta la palabra hebrea o griega exacta detrás de ella, luego asignar a cada palabra hebrea y a cada palabra griega un número único que cualquier lector que solo conociera el inglés pudiera usar. Quería poner las lenguas originales en la mano del arador del campo.

blocks.en: It took him twenty-seven years. He worked nights and weekends while teaching full-time at Drew. He recruited over a hundred volunteer assistants. He cross-checked every entry against multiple ancient manuscripts. When Strong's Exhaustive Concordance of the Bible finally went to press in 1890, it was the size of a city telephone directory. It listed every English word in the KJV in alphabetical order, every verse where that word appeared, and beside each verse the unique number that pointed to the Hebrew or Greek word underneath. The Hebrew side ran from H1 (av, "father") to H8674. The Greek side ran from G1 (Alpha) to G5624. In the back of the book were two dictionaries — a Hebrew lexicon and a Greek lexicon — arranged numerically. Any English-speaking believer could now look up a verse, see the Strong's number beside the word, flip to the back, and read what the Hebrew or Greek actually meant. The seminary had been moved into the hand of the layman.
blocks.es_reference: Le tomó veintisiete años. Trabajó noches y fines de semana mientras enseñaba tiempo completo en Drew. Reclutó más de cien asistentes voluntarios. Cotejó cada entrada contra múltiples manuscritos antiguos. Cuando La Concordancia Exhaustiva de Strong de la Biblia finalmente fue a imprenta en 1890, tenía el tamaño de un directorio telefónico de ciudad. Listaba cada palabra inglesa de la KJV en orden alfabético, cada versículo donde aparecía esa palabra, y junto a cada versículo el número único que apuntaba a la palabra hebrea o griega subyacente. El lado hebreo iba de H1 (av, «padre») a H8674. El lado griego iba de G1 (Alfa) a G5624. Al final del libro había dos diccionarios — un lexicón hebreo y un lexicón griego — ordenados numéricamente. Cualquier creyente de habla inglesa podía ahora buscar un versículo, ver el número de Strong junto a la palabra, voltear al final, y leer lo que el hebreo o griego realmente significaba. El seminario se había movido a la mano del laico.

blocks.en: For 1,800 years the Hebrew and Greek originals had been locked behind seminary walls. In 1890 a Methodist professor handed the key to anyone who would pick it up.
blocks.es_reference: Por 1,800 años los originales hebreos y griegos habían estado encerrados detrás de las paredes del seminario. En 1890 un profesor metodista entregó la llave a cualquiera que la tomara.

blocks.en: The Wycliffe-Tyndale tradition
blocks.es_reference: La tradición Wycliffe-Tyndale

blocks.en: Strong did not invent democratizing Scripture. He stood on a long line. John Wycliffe in the 1380s translated the whole Bible into Middle English so that every English peasant could read it. William Tyndale in the 1520s did the same for early modern English — and was strangled and burned for his trouble at Vilvoorde in 1536. His dying prayer, "Lord, open the King of England's eyes," was answered within three years when Henry VIII authorized the Great Bible in 1539. Alexander Cruden in 1737 compiled the first great English concordance, working from a London garret, in and out of asylums for the rest of his eccentric life, but producing a tool that put every verse at the fingertips of every Bible reader. Strong's concordance of 1890 is the next step in that line. Each generation has chipped away at the wall between the ordinary Christian and the original Word of God. Strong's number system was the largest hammer of them all.
blocks.es_reference: Strong no inventó el democratizar las Escrituras. Estuvo parado sobre una larga línea. Juan Wycliffe en los 1380s tradujo toda la Biblia al inglés medio para que cada campesino inglés pudiera leerla. William Tyndale en los 1520s hizo lo mismo para el inglés moderno temprano — y fue estrangulado y quemado por sus problemas en Vilvoorde en 1536. Su oración moribunda, «Señor, abre los ojos del Rey de Inglaterra», fue respondida dentro de tres años cuando Enrique VIII autorizó la Gran Biblia en 1539. Alexander Cruden en 1737 compiló la primera gran concordancia inglesa, trabajando desde un ático de Londres, entrando y saliendo de manicomios durante el resto de su excéntrica vida, pero produciendo una herramienta que puso cada versículo al alcance de cada lector de la Biblia. La concordancia de Strong de 1890 es el siguiente paso en esa línea. Cada generación ha cincelado la pared entre el cristiano ordinario y la Palabra original de Dios. El sistema de números de Strong fue el martillo más grande de todos.

blocks.en: Why this unit matters
blocks.es_reference: Por qué importa esta unidad

blocks.en: Units 1 through 9 gave you a map of the territory: the textual story (Units 1–2), the Hebrew alphabet (Units 3–4), the Hebrew word treasures (Unit 5), the Greek alphabet (Units 6–7), and eight great Greek words for salvation (Units 8–9). You have seen what is possible. Unit 10 hands you the tool that lets you do this for yourself, for any word in any verse, for the rest of your life. By the end of this lesson you will know how to use Strong's numbers in three forms: on paper (the original concordance), on a phone (the modern apps), and on the full internet (Bible study websites). Unit 11 will then turn you loose on your first real word study. You are almost at the finish.
blocks.es_reference: Las Unidades 1 a 9 te dieron un mapa del territorio: la historia textual (Unidades 1–2), el alfabeto hebreo (Unidades 3–4), los tesoros de palabras hebreas (Unidad 5), el alfabeto griego (Unidades 6–7), y ocho grandes palabras griegas para la salvación (Unidades 8–9). Has visto lo que es posible. La Unidad 10 te entrega la herramienta que te permite hacer esto tú mismo, para cualquier palabra en cualquier versículo, por el resto de tu vida. Para el final de esta lección sabrás cómo usar los números de Strong en tres formas: en papel (la concordancia original), en teléfono (las aplicaciones modernas), y en internet completo (sitios de estudio bíblico). La Unidad 11 luego te soltará en tu primer estudio real de palabras. Casi llegas a la meta.

blocks.en: Our unit scripture is 2 Timothy 2:15. The English word "study" here translates the Greek spoudazô (Strong's G4704), which actually means "be diligent, give earnest effort." Paul is not telling Timothy to read more. He is telling Timothy to work hard at handling the Word. The phrase "rightly dividing" translates orthotomeô (Strong's G3718), "cut straight." Paul is telling Timothy to cut a straight line through Scripture like a stonemason cutting a stone or a tailor cutting cloth. Strong's numbers are the workman's tool. They do not make you a workman; they equip the workman you already want to be.
blocks.es_reference: Nuestra escritura de la unidad es 2 Timoteo 2:15. La palabra inglesa «study» (procura con diligencia) traduce el griego spoudazô (número de Strong G4704), que en realidad significa «ser diligente, dar esfuerzo serio». Pablo no está diciendo a Timoteo que lea más. Le está diciendo a Timoteo que trabaje duro en el manejo de la Palabra. La frase «trazar bien» traduce orthotomeô (número de Strong G3718), «cortar derecho». Pablo le está diciendo a Timoteo que corte una línea recta a través de la Escritura como un albañil cortando una piedra o un sastre cortando tela. Los números de Strong son la herramienta del obrero. No te hacen un obrero; equipan al obrero que ya quieres ser.

blocks.en: I. How Strong's Works: The Original Paper Concordance
blocks.es_reference: I. Cómo funciona Strong: La concordancia original en papel

blocks.en: Imagine you have a hardcover copy of Strong's Exhaustive Concordance on your desk. (You will not have one in Mexico unless someone shipped it to you, but the structure is identical online and on your phone, so understanding the paper version teaches you how every digital tool works.) Open the concordance and you find three main parts:
blocks.es_reference: Imagina que tienes una copia de tapa dura de la Concordancia Exhaustiva de Strong en tu escritorio. (No tendrás una en México a menos que alguien te la haya enviado, pero la estructura es idéntica en línea y en tu teléfono, así que entender la versión en papel te enseña cómo funciona cada herramienta digital.) Abre la concordancia y encuentras tres partes principales:

blocks.en: <th>Part</th><th>What it contains</th>
blocks.es_reference: <th>Parte</th><th>Lo que contiene</th>

blocks.en: Main concordanceEvery English word in the KJV in alphabetical order. Under each word, every verse where it appears, with the Strong's number beside each occurrence.
blocks.es_reference: Concordancia principalCada palabra inglesa de la KJV en orden alfabético. Bajo cada palabra, cada versículo donde aparece, con el número de Strong junto a cada ocurrencia.

blocks.en: Hebrew dictionary (back)Numbers H1 through H8674. Each number is one Hebrew word, with a brief definition, etymology, and list of how the KJV translates it.
blocks.es_reference: Diccionario hebreo (al final)Números H1 a H8674. Cada número es una palabra hebrea, con una definición breve, etimología, y lista de cómo la KJV la traduce.

blocks.en: Greek dictionary (back)Numbers G1 through G5624. Each number is one Greek word, with a brief definition, etymology, and list of how the KJV translates it.
blocks.es_reference: Diccionario griego (al final)Números G1 a G5624. Cada número es una palabra griega, con una definición breve, etimología, y lista de cómo la KJV la traduce.

blocks.en: The lookup process is four steps. Step one: find your verse in the main concordance under any meaningful word in it. Suppose you are studying John 3:16, "For God so loved the world …" Look up the word "loved." Step two: scan the list of every occurrence of "loved" in the KJV until you find John 3:16. Step three: note the Strong's number printed next to that occurrence. For "loved" in John 3:16 the number is G25. The "G" tells you Greek (NT); a "H" would tell you Hebrew (OT). Step four: flip to the Greek dictionary at the back, find entry G25, and read the lexical information: agapaô, the verb form of the noun agapê you learned in Unit 8. Self-giving sacrificial love. The same root that Christ used when He commanded us to love our enemies.
blocks.es_reference: El proceso de búsqueda son cuatro pasos. Paso uno: encuentra tu versículo en la concordancia principal bajo cualquier palabra significativa en él. Supongamos que estás estudiando Juan 3:16, «Porque de tal manera amó Dios al mundo …» Busca la palabra «amó». Paso dos: recorre la lista de cada ocurrencia de «amó» en la KJV hasta que encuentres Juan 3:16. Paso tres: nota el número de Strong impreso junto a esa ocurrencia. Para «amó» en Juan 3:16 el número es G25. La «G» te dice griego (NT); una «H» te diría hebreo (AT). Paso cuatro: voltea al diccionario griego al final, encuentra la entrada G25, y lee la información léxica: agapaô, la forma verbal del sustantivo agapê que aprendiste en la Unidad 8. Amor sacrificial abnegado. La misma raíz que Cristo usó cuando nos mandó amar a nuestros enemigos.

blocks.en: The whole process takes about ninety seconds once you know the rhythm. And the payoff is that you have just done what only seminary professors could do a hundred and fifty years ago. You have read John 3:16 in Greek without learning Greek grammar. Strong's number G25 was the bridge.
blocks.es_reference: Todo el proceso toma unos noventa segundos una vez que conoces el ritmo. Y la recompensa es que acabas de hacer lo que solo profesores de seminario podían hacer hace ciento cincuenta años. Has leído Juan 3:16 en griego sin aprender gramática griega. El número de Strong G25 fue el puente.

blocks.en: One warning, repeated
blocks.es_reference: Una advertencia, repetida

blocks.en: Strong's gives you a brief lexical entry — usually one or two sentences. It is a starting point, not the last word. Many serious Bible students go on to use larger lexicons like Thayer's (Greek) or Brown-Driver-Briggs (Hebrew). Both of these are keyed to Strong's numbers, so once you know how to find a Strong's number, you can look the same word up in any major lexicon. The number is the bridge. Once across the bridge, there is a whole library waiting.
blocks.es_reference: Strong te da una entrada léxica breve — usualmente una o dos oraciones. Es un punto de partida, no la última palabra. Muchos estudiantes serios de la Biblia siguen usando lexicones más grandes como Thayer (griego) o Brown-Driver-Briggs (hebreo). Ambos están numerados a los números de Strong, así que una vez que sepas cómo encontrar un número de Strong, puedes buscar la misma palabra en cualquier lexicón principal. El número es el puente. Una vez al otro lado del puente, hay toda una biblioteca esperando.

blocks.en: II. Strong's on a Phone: The Apps
blocks.es_reference: II. Strong en un teléfono: Las aplicaciones

blocks.en: Most students in our seminary will never own the paper concordance. You do not need to. The same content is in your pocket. Several free or low-cost mobile apps put Strong's numbers, full lexicons, and parallel Bible translations on your phone. Here are the four most reliable choices for an English-or-Spanish-speaking believer in Mexico in this decade:
blocks.es_reference: La mayoría de los estudiantes en nuestro seminario nunca poseerán la concordancia en papel. No la necesitas. El mismo contenido está en tu bolsillo. Varias aplicaciones móviles gratuitas o de bajo costo ponen los números de Strong, lexicones completos, y traducciones bíblicas paralelas en tu teléfono. Aquí están las cuatro opciones más confiables para un creyente de habla inglesa o española en México en esta década:

blocks.en: <th>App</th><th>Platforms</th><th>Cost</th><th>What it gives you</th>

blocks.es_reference: MySword (Android) / PocketSword (iOS)Solo móvilGratisLigera, rápida, gratis. Búsqueda de Strong incorporada. Muchos módulos gratuitos para uso sin conexión, importante cuando el WiFi es inestable.

blocks.es_reference: Logos Bible (aplicación móvil)iOS, Android, escritorioApp gratis; biblioteca de pagoLa herramienta de grado profesional. La aplicación gratuita da algo de Strong; los módulos serios cuestan dinero. Adecuado para pastores que quieren profundidad.

blocks.en: The workflow on a phone is even faster than paper. Open Blue Letter Bible. Type the verse reference (John 3:16). Tap the word "loved." A pop-up appears showing the Strong's number (G25), the Greek word (agapaô), the lexicon entry, the verse list, and a play button to hear it pronounced. Three taps, ten seconds, and you are inside the Greek. The man who took twenty-seven years to compile this in 1890 would have wept at how quickly his work now serves you.
blocks.es_reference: El flujo de trabajo en un teléfono es aún más rápido que el papel. Abre Blue Letter Bible. Escribe la referencia del versículo (Juan 3:16). Toca la palabra «amó». Aparece una ventana emergente que muestra el número de Strong (G25), la palabra griega (agapaô), la entrada del lexicón, la lista de versículos, y un botón de reproducción para oírla pronunciada. Tres toques, diez segundos, y estás dentro del griego. El hombre que tomó veintisiete años para compilar esto en 1890 habría llorado por la rapidez con que su trabajo ahora te sirve.

blocks.en: Spanish-language note
blocks.es_reference: Nota sobre el español

blocks.en: Most of the Strong's-keyed tools are still in English first, Spanish second. The Reina-Valera 1960 keyed to Strong's numbers is available in both Blue Letter Bible and e-Sword. The Reina-Valera Gomez (RVG) does not yet have a fully Strong's-keyed module in every app, so when working in Spanish you may want to consult parallel English-Spanish texts. The Strong's numbers themselves are language-neutral — G25 is G25 whether you read Juan 3:16 or John 3:16.
blocks.es_reference: La mayoría de las herramientas numeradas a Strong todavía están primero en inglés y luego en español. La Reina-Valera 1960 numerada a los números de Strong está disponible tanto en Blue Letter Bible como en e-Sword. La Reina-Valera Gómez (RVG) todavía no tiene un módulo completamente numerado a Strong en cada aplicación, así que cuando trabajes en español querrás consultar textos paralelos inglés-español. Los números de Strong mismos son neutros respecto al idioma — G25 es G25 ya sea que leas Juan 3:16 o John 3:16.

blocks.en: III. Strong's on the Full Internet: The Free Websites
blocks.es_reference: III. Strong en internet completo: Los sitios web gratuitos

blocks.en: When you sit at a real computer with a real web browser, you have access to tools more powerful than any printed concordance ever produced. The best of these are free and require no registration. Here are the four that every workman in the Word should bookmark today:
blocks.es_reference: Cuando te sientas en una computadora real con un navegador web real, tienes acceso a herramientas más poderosas que cualquier concordancia impresa jamás producida. Las mejores son gratuitas y no requieren registro. Aquí están las cuatro que cada obrero en la Palabra debe marcar como favorito hoy:

blocks.en: <th>Site</th><th>URL</th><th>What it gives you</th>

blocks.es_reference: Blue Letter Bibleblueletterbible.orgEl mismo contenido que la aplicación, en el escritorio. Pasa el cursor sobre cualquier palabra en cualquier versículo para obtener el número de Strong, griego/hebreo, entrada del lexicón, y enlaces a cada otro uso en la Escritura.

blocks.es_reference: Bible Hubbiblehub.comInterlineal versículo por versículo con inglés, griego, transliteración, Strong, análisis gramatical, y traducciones paralelas todo en una pantalla. El mejor interlineal gratuito en la web.

blocks.en: For a Mexican student of Wayne's seminary, Blue Letter Bible and Bible Hub are the two essentials. Both are free, both work in Spanish-language browsers, both keep their data up to date, both pair with the underlying lexicons (Thayer's for Greek, Brown-Driver-Briggs for Hebrew). If you can use only one tool, use Blue Letter Bible. If you can use two, add Bible Hub for the interlinear view.
blocks.es_reference: Para un estudiante mexicano del seminario de Wayne, Blue Letter Bible y Bible Hub son los dos esenciales. Ambos son gratuitos, ambos funcionan en navegadores de habla española, ambos mantienen sus datos actualizados, ambos se emparejan con los lexicones subyacentes (Thayer para griego, Brown-Driver-Briggs para hebreo). Si solo puedes usar una herramienta, usa Blue Letter Bible. Si puedes usar dos, agrega Bible Hub para la vista interlineal.

blocks.en: A worked example: Romans 1:17
blocks.es_reference: Un ejemplo trabajado: Romanos 1:17

blocks.en: Let us do live what Luther did in 1516. Open biblehub.com in your browser. Type "Romans 1:17" in the search box. Click "Interlinear." You see the entire verse displayed word by word: English on top, then the Greek word, then the transliteration, then the Strong's number, then the grammatical parsing. Find the English word "righteousness." Beneath it is the Greek dikaiosynê, transliteration "dikaiosunê," Strong's number G1343, parsing "noun, nominative, feminine, singular." Click the G1343 link. You jump to the lexicon entry, which gives Thayer's full discussion of the word. Read it. You have just done the Luther exercise. You have read Romans 1:17 in Greek, looked up the key word in the standard Greek lexicon, and understood why the verse means "the righteousness God GIVES" and not "the standard God demands." Five centuries after Luther, the same insight is one mouse click away.
blocks.es_reference: Hagamos en vivo lo que Lutero hizo en 1516. Abre biblehub.com en tu navegador. Escribe «Romans 1:17» en la caja de búsqueda. Haz clic en «Interlinear». Ves todo el versículo desplegado palabra por palabra: inglés arriba, luego la palabra griega, luego la transliteración, luego el número de Strong, luego el análisis gramatical. Encuentra la palabra inglesa «righteousness» (justicia). Debajo está el griego dikaiosynê, transliteración «dikaiosunê», número de Strong G1343, análisis «sustantivo, nominativo, femenino, singular». Haz clic en el enlace G1343. Saltas a la entrada del lexicón, que da la discusión completa de Thayer de la palabra. Léela. Acabas de hacer el ejercicio de Lutero. Has leído Romanos 1:17 en griego, buscado la palabra clave en el lexicón griego estándar, y entendido por qué el versículo significa «la justicia que Dios DA» y no «el estándar que Dios exige». Cinco siglos después de Lutero, la misma intuición está a un clic de ratón.

blocks.en: Five centuries ago Luther had to be a Hebrew and Greek scholar to discover this. Today any English-speaking believer with a phone can replicate his discovery in thirty seconds.
blocks.es_reference: Hace cinco siglos Lutero tenía que ser un erudito hebreo y griego para descubrir esto. Hoy cualquier creyente con un teléfono puede replicar su descubrimiento en treinta segundos.

blocks.en: IV. Three Pitfalls Every Workman Must Avoid
blocks.es_reference: IV. Tres trampas que todo obrero debe evitar

blocks.en: A power tool in the hand of an untrained workman is dangerous. Strong's numbers in the hand of a careless student have produced thousands of sincere but wrong sermons over the past century. Before we set you loose on Unit 11, you need to know the three classic mistakes and how to avoid them. None of them are problems with Strong's itself. All of them are problems with how the workman uses the tool.
blocks.es_reference: Una herramienta poderosa en la mano de un obrero sin entrenamiento es peligrosa. Los números de Strong en la mano de un estudiante descuidado han producido miles de sermones sinceros pero erróneos durante el siglo pasado. Antes de soltarte en la Unidad 11, necesitas conocer los tres errores clásicos y cómo evitarlos. Ninguno de ellos es un problema con Strong en sí. Todos son problemas con cómo el obrero usa la herramienta.

blocks.en: Pitfall 1: The root fallacy. The assumption that the original meaning of a word's root is what the word "really" means in any later passage. Example: someone preaches "the church is dynamite!" from dynamis (Greek "power," from which we get the English word "dynamite") in Acts 1:8. But dynamis was used in Greek for five hundred years before dynamite was invented in 1867. The Greek word means "power" or "ability." It has nothing to do with explosives. The English derivative is fun trivia but bad exegesis. The rule: a word's meaning is determined by how it is used in its own period and context, not by where the word originally came from.
blocks.es_reference: Trampa 1: La falacia de la raíz. La suposición de que el significado original de la raíz de una palabra es lo que la palabra «realmente» significa en cualquier pasaje posterior. Ejemplo: alguien predica «¡la iglesia es dinamita!» desde dynamis (griego «poder», de donde obtenemos la palabra inglesa «dinamita») en Hechos 1:8. Pero dynamis se usó en griego por quinientos años antes de que la dinamita fuera inventada en 1867. La palabra griega significa «poder» o «habilidad». No tiene nada que ver con explosivos. El derivado en inglés es trivia divertida pero mala exégesis. La regla: el significado de una palabra está determinado por cómo se usa en su propio período y contexto, no por de dónde vino originalmente.

blocks.en: Pitfall 2: The illegitimate totality transfer. The assumption that a Greek or Hebrew word always means everything its lexicon entry lists, all at once, in every passage. Sôzô can mean rescue from drowning, rescue from disease, rescue from death, or rescue from sin (Unit 9 covered this). But in any single verse it usually means one of those things, not all four at once. The rule: the lexicon gives you the range of possible meanings; the context tells you which one the author intended in this verse.
blocks.es_reference: Trampa 2: La transferencia ilegítima de totalidad. La suposición de que una palabra griega o hebrea siempre significa todo lo que enumera su entrada en el lexicón, todo a la vez, en cada pasaje. Sôzô puede significar rescatar de ahogarse, rescatar de enfermedad, rescatar de muerte, o rescatar de pecado (la Unidad 9 cubrió esto). Pero en cualquier versículo individual usualmente significa una de esas cosas, no las cuatro a la vez. La regla: el lexicón te da el rango de significados posibles; el contexto te dice cuál intentaba el autor en este versículo.

blocks.en: Pitfall 3: The "deeper meaning" trap. The assumption that learning the Greek or Hebrew always reveals a "hidden" or "deeper" meaning that the English translation missed. Usually this is not true. Most modern translations are made by careful scholars who know far more Greek and Hebrew than any of us ever will. The English already captures 95% of what the Greek says. Word study deepens 5%, sharpens edges, and prevents misreadings — it does not normally overturn the meaning of the verse. The rule: Strong's enriches; Strong's does not normally correct your English Bible.
blocks.es_reference: Trampa 3: La trampa del «significado más profundo». La suposición de que aprender el griego o el hebreo siempre revela un significado «oculto» o «más profundo» que la traducción inglesa o castellana perdió. Usualmente esto no es verdad. La mayoría de las traducciones modernas son hechas por eruditos cuidadosos que saben más griego y hebreo que cualquiera de nosotros jamás sabrá. El español ya captura el 95% de lo que el griego dice. El estudio de palabras profundiza el 5%, afila los bordes, y previene malas lecturas — normalmente no revierte el significado del versículo. La regla: Strong enriquece; Strong normalmente no corrige tu Biblia.

blocks.en: The Berean attitude (Acts 17:11)
blocks.es_reference: La actitud bereana (Hechos 17:11)

blocks.en: When Paul preached at Berea, Luke records that the Bereans were "more noble … in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so." The Greek word for "searched" is anakrinô (Strong's G350), a courtroom verb meaning "to examine carefully, to investigate, to cross-examine." The Bereans loved Paul, but they did not take even his preaching at face value. They opened their Old Testament scrolls and checked his claims against the inspired text. This is the attitude that Strong's enables for every layperson. You no longer need to take any preacher's word for what the Greek says. You can anakrinô the claim. You can check it for yourself. Strong's numbers are the modern equivalent of the Berean's scroll.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Pablo predicó en Berea, Lucas registra que los bereanos eran «más nobles … pues recibieron la palabra con toda solicitud, escudriñando cada día las Escrituras para ver si estas cosas eran así». La palabra griega para «escudriñar» es anakrinô (número de Strong G350), un verbo de tribunal que significa «examinar cuidadosamente, investigar, interrogar». Los bereanos amaban a Pablo, pero no tomaron ni siquiera su predicación al pie de la letra. Abrieron sus rollos del Antiguo Testamento y verificaron sus afirmaciones contra el texto inspirado. Esta es la actitud que Strong habilita para cada laico. Ya no necesitas tomar la palabra de ningún predicador sobre lo que dice el griego. Puedes anakrinô la afirmación. Puedes verificarla por ti mismo. Los números de Strong son el equivalente moderno del rollo bereano.

blocks.en: Strong's makes every Christian a Berean. It hands the cross-examination tool to the layperson in the pew. A preacher who fears Strong's-equipped congregations is a preacher with something to hide.
blocks.es_reference: Strong hace de cada cristiano un bereano. Pone la herramienta de interrogatorio en la mano del laico en la banca. Un predicador que teme a las congregaciones equipadas con Strong es un predicador con algo que esconder.

blocks.en: V. Putting It Together — and the Bridge to Unit 11
blocks.es_reference: V. Poniendo todo junto — y el puente a la Unidad 11

blocks.en: You have now seen Strong's numbers in three forms. Paper for the historic foundation, phone for the daily workman, internet for the deep dive. All three contain the same essential content: every Hebrew and Greek word in the Bible keyed to a number, with a brief definition, and a list of every verse where the word appears. That single innovation — one number per word — broke down the wall between the seminary and the laity in 1890 and is still doing it in 2026.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora has visto los números de Strong en tres formas. Papel para el fundamento histórico, teléfono para el obrero diario, internet para la inmersión profunda. Las tres contienen el mismo contenido esencial: cada palabra hebrea y griega en la Biblia numerada, con una definición breve, y una lista de cada versículo donde aparece la palabra. Esa única innovación — un número por palabra — rompió la pared entre el seminario y los laicos en 1890 y todavía lo está haciendo en 2026.

blocks.en: What a complete Strong's word study looks like
blocks.es_reference: Cómo se ve un estudio de palabras Strong completo

blocks.en: Here is the workflow you will apply in Unit 11. Pick a verse. Pick a key word in that verse. Look up the Strong's number. Read the lexicon entry. Look up every other place the same Strong's number appears in Scripture. Read those other verses, noting how the same word is used in different contexts. Now go back to your original verse and reread it with all of that in your mind. You have just done a real word study. The whole process takes fifteen minutes in Blue Letter Bible. It used to take a seminary degree.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí está el flujo de trabajo que aplicarás en la Unidad 11. Elige un versículo. Elige una palabra clave en ese versículo. Busca el número de Strong. Lee la entrada del lexicón. Busca cada otro lugar donde el mismo número de Strong aparece en la Escritura. Lee esos otros versículos, notando cómo se usa la misma palabra en diferentes contextos. Ahora regresa a tu versículo original y reléelo con todo eso en tu mente. Acabas de hacer un estudio de palabras real. Todo el proceso toma quince minutos en Blue Letter Bible. Solía tomar un grado del seminario.

blocks.en: Before you take the examination, do this. Pick any verse from Romans 5 that contains a word you would like to understand more deeply. Open Blue Letter Bible (web or phone). Find the Strong's number. Read the lexicon. List every other occurrence of the same Strong's number in Romans (just Romans, not all of Scripture — we are keeping this short). Write three sentences in your notebook: (1) the word and its Strong's number, (2) the dictionary meaning, (3) how seeing the word's other uses changes or deepens your reading of your original verse. Save this. You will turn in a longer version like it as your Unit 11 word-study project.
blocks.es_reference: Antes de tomar el examen, haz esto. Elige cualquier versículo de Romanos 5 que contenga una palabra que te gustaría entender más profundamente. Abre Blue Letter Bible (web o teléfono). Encuentra el número de Strong. Lee el lexicón. Enumera cada otra ocurrencia del mismo número de Strong en Romanos (solo Romanos, no toda la Escritura — estamos manteniéndolo corto). Escribe tres oraciones en tu cuaderno: (1) la palabra y su número de Strong, (2) el significado del diccionario, (3) cómo ver los otros usos de la palabra cambia o profundiza tu lectura de tu versículo original. Guarda esto. Entregarás una versión más larga como tu proyecto de estudio de palabras de la Unidad 11.

blocks.en: What Unit 11 will require
blocks.es_reference: Lo que requerirá la Unidad 11

blocks.en: Unit 11 is the capstone of the entire Language Appreciation course. You will choose one Greek word from the New Testament that has appeared somewhere in Units 5 through 9 (or another word approved by Wayne). You will use Strong's numbers and Blue Letter Bible to perform a full word study, write it up in approximately 800 words, and present your findings. You will trace the word's lexical meaning, its uses across the New Testament, any Old Testament Hebrew word it translates (if applicable), and how it shapes the doctrine of the passage in which you found it. The course you are nearly done with has prepared you to do this well. Unit 11 is where you prove you can use what you have been given. One unit left. You can see the finish line.
blocks.es_reference: La Unidad 11 es el remate de todo el curso de Apreciación de Lenguas Bíblicas. Elegirás una palabra griega del Nuevo Testamento que haya aparecido en alguna parte en las Unidades 5 a 9 (u otra palabra aprobada por Wayne). Usarás los números de Strong y Blue Letter Bible para realizar un estudio de palabras completo, escribirlo en aproximadamente 800 palabras, y presentar tus hallazgos. El curso que estás casi terminando te ha preparado para hacer esto bien. La Unidad 11 es donde demuestras que puedes usar lo que se te ha dado. Una unidad queda. Puedes ver la meta.

blocks.en: 📚 Catalog / Catálogo

mc.stem: Who compiled Strong's Exhaustive Concordance of the Bible, and in what year was it first published?
options: James Strong, professor at Drew Theological Seminary, published in 1890 after twenty-seven years of work
Alexander Cruden, a London printer, published in 1737
William Tyndale, the English martyr, published in 1525
Joseph Thayer, professor at Harvard, published in 1886
mc.why: James Strong (1822–1894) was professor of Hebrew and Greek at Drew Theological Seminary in New Jersey. He began compiling his concordance in 1863, recruited over 100 volunteer assistants, and saw it through twenty-seven years of work to publication in 1890. The resulting volume listed every English word of the KJV with the Hebrew or Greek word behind it, each numbered uniquely. The seminary went into the hand of the layman.

mc.stem: What range of numbers does Strong's assign to Hebrew words, and what range to Greek words?
options: Hebrew 1–1000, Greek 1–1000 — both capped at one thousand
Hebrew and Greek share one number sequence from 1 to 13000
Hebrew H1–H8674 and Greek G1–G5624
Hebrew H1–H10000 and Greek G1–G10000 — both rounded to ten thousand
mc.why: Strong's Hebrew dictionary runs from H1 (av, 'father') to H8674. The Greek dictionary runs from G1 (Alpha) to G5624. The H or G prefix tells you which language. So G3056 is logos, G4982 is sôzô, G2962 is kyrios, G1343 is dikaiosynê, G4102 is pistis. Every Hebrew and Greek word in the Bible has a unique number.

mc.stem: James Strong's work is part of a centuries-long line of efforts to give the Bible to the ordinary believer. Which of the following figures DOES NOT belong to that line?
options: John Wycliffe (1380s, first complete English Bible)
William Tyndale (1520s, first printed English NT; martyred 1536)
Alexander Cruden (1737, first major English concordance)
Genghis Khan (1200s, Mongol emperor)
mc.why: Wycliffe, Tyndale, and Cruden all worked to put Scripture or scriptural tools in the hand of the common believer. Strong's 1890 concordance stands in that same democratizing tradition. Genghis Khan, while historically remarkable, did not contribute to making Scripture accessible.

mc.stem: In our unit scripture, 2 Timothy 2:15, what does the Greek word spoudazô (Strong's G4704, translated 'study' in the KJV) actually mean?
options: To memorize verses by rote
To read silently in a library
To attend formal academic classes
To be diligent, to give earnest effort, to work hard at handling the Word
mc.why: Spoudazô means 'be diligent, make every effort, hasten, work hard.' The English 'study' has narrowed in modern usage to 'reading at a desk,' but the Greek is more active — Paul is commanding Timothy to work hard at being a workman with the Word. Strong's numbers immediately put this nuance in your hand.

mc.stem: In 2 Timothy 2:15 the phrase 'rightly dividing' translates the Greek orthotomeô (Strong's G3718). What is the literal meaning of this Greek verb?
options: To pray quietly
To cut straight, like a stonemason cutting a stone or a tailor cutting cloth
To memorize entire chapters
To debate publicly
mc.why: Orthotomeô is built from orthos ('straight') + tomê ('cut'). It means literally 'to cut straight,' a workman's image. Paul is telling Timothy to handle Scripture the way a craftsman cuts stone or fabric — with clean, intentional, accurate work. Strong's gives you this image instantly; the English 'rightly dividing' is good but loses the craftsman picture.

mc.stem: What is the four-step lookup process for using a paper Strong's concordance?
options: Find your verse in the main concordance under a meaningful word; locate your verse in that word's list; note the Strong's number; flip to the Hebrew or Greek dictionary at the back to read the lexical entry
Recite the Apostles' Creed, then sing a hymn, then read your verse, then pray
Memorize the Hebrew alphabet, then the Greek alphabet, then translate the verse word-by-word
Email a seminary professor and wait for him to respond with the Greek meaning
mc.why: The four steps: (1) find your verse in the main alphabetical concordance under a meaningful word, (2) locate your specific verse in the list of occurrences, (3) note the Strong's number printed beside it, (4) flip to the Hebrew or Greek dictionary at the back and read the lexical entry. Once you know the rhythm, the whole process takes about ninety seconds on paper, ten seconds on a phone.

mc.stem: In John 3:16 ('For God so loved the world'), the English word 'loved' has Strong's number G25. To which Greek word does this number point?
options: phileô — the love of friendship between equals
erôs — romantic, passionate, desire-based love
agapaô — the verb form of agapê, self-giving sacrificial love
storgê — family affection between parent and child
mc.why: G25 is agapaô, the verb form of agapê that you learned in Unit 8. The 'love' of John 3:16 is self-giving sacrificial agapê — the love that crosses every tribe, gives without return, and seeks the good of an enemy. Without Strong's, an English-only reader has no way to know which of the four Greek words for love stands behind 'loved' in his English Bible. G25 is the bridge.

mc.stem: Which free mobile app is the most universally recommended Strong's-keyed Bible tool for English- and Spanish-speaking students today?
options: TikTok
Blue Letter Bible — free, Strong's built in, lexicon entries, audio pronunciation
WhatsApp
Google Translate
mc.why: Blue Letter Bible is the universal recommendation: free, works on iOS, Android, and the web, every English (and many Spanish) word tappable for instant Strong's number and lexicon entry, with audio pronunciation. Tap a word and you are inside the Greek or Hebrew in seconds. If a student installs only one app from this unit, it should be Blue Letter Bible.

mc.stem: Which free website provides the best verse-by-verse English-Greek interlinear with Strong's numbers, parsing, and parallel translations all on one screen?
options: Wikipedia
Facebook
YouTube
Bible Hub (biblehub.com)
mc.why: Bible Hub (biblehub.com) is the single best free interlinear on the web. Every verse appears word-by-word with the original Greek or Hebrew, transliteration, Strong's number, full grammatical parsing, and several parallel English translations. Click any Strong's number and you jump directly to the Thayer's or BDB lexicon entry. Free, no registration, indispensable for any serious word study.

mc.stem: What does 'the root fallacy' mean in word-study work?
options: The mistake of using a tree-root metaphor in a sermon
The mistake of believing the Hebrew Bible is rootless

The mistake of assuming the original meaning of a word's root is what the word 'really' means in any later passage — for example, preaching that 'the church is dynamite' because dynamis ('power') gives us the English word dynamite (which wasn't invented until 1867)
The mistake of failing to memorize Hebrew word roots
mc.why: The root fallacy assumes the etymological root or English derivative reveals the 'true' meaning of the Greek or Hebrew word. The classic example: 'dynamis (Acts 1:8) means dynamite-power' — but dynamite was invented in 1867; the Greek word means 'power, ability' in its own first-century context, with no explosive connotation. Strong's number doesn't make this mistake; careless preachers do. Rule: a word's meaning is determined by how it is used in its own period and context, not by where it originally came from or what later English word derives from it.

mc.stem: What is 'the illegitimate totality transfer' in word-study work?
options: The assumption that a Greek or Hebrew word always means everything its lexicon entry lists, all at once, in every passage — even though context usually selects only one meaning at a time
The transfer of Greek words into Hebrew translation
The illegal copying of copyrighted Bible commentaries
The transfer of seminary students between schools
mc.why: The illegitimate totality transfer is the assumption that every nuance the lexicon lists for a word is operative in every passage. Sôzô can mean 'rescue from drowning, disease, death, shipwreck, or sin' — but in any single verse it usually means one of those, not all five at once. The lexicon gives you the RANGE; context tells you which meaning the author intended HERE. This is the mature workman's discipline.

mc.stem: Why is it incorrect to assume that learning the Greek behind an English verse will always reveal a 'hidden' or 'deeper' meaning the English missed?
options: Because the Greek text has been lost

Because most modern translations are made by careful scholars who know far more Greek and Hebrew than any of us — the English (or Spanish) already captures most of what the original says, so Strong's normally enriches and sharpens rather than overturning the translation
Because the Greek New Testament was rewritten in the Middle Ages
Because Hebrew and Greek are now extinct languages
mc.why: The 'deeper meaning' trap assumes Bible translators are hiding something. They almost never are. Modern translation committees include the most accomplished Hebrew and Greek scholars alive. The English Bible already says about 95% of what the original says. Strong's deepens the remaining 5%, sharpens edges, prevents misreadings, and supplies the cultural and lexical context an English word loses — but it normally does not overturn the meaning of the verse.

mc.stem: In Acts 17:11 the Bereans are called more noble because they 'searched the Scriptures daily.' The Greek verb is anakrinô (Strong's G350). What does this verb mean?
options: A courtroom verb meaning 'to examine carefully, to investigate, to cross-examine'
A military verb meaning 'to march in formation'
A musical verb meaning 'to sing in harmony'
An agricultural verb meaning 'to harvest grain'
mc.why: Anakrinô (G350) is a legal verb meaning 'to examine carefully, to investigate, to cross-examine.' The Bereans loved Paul but did not take even his preaching at face value. They opened their Old Testament scrolls and cross-examined his claims against the inspired text. Strong's makes every modern Christian a Berean: a layperson with the cross-examination tool now in hand. A preacher who fears Strong's-equipped congregations has something to hide.

mc.stem: What are the three forms in which a modern student can use Strong's numbers, as taught in Unit 10?
options: Whispered in Latin, chanted in Greek, sung in Hebrew
Memorized, recited, dramatized
Only the paper concordance is reliable; phones and websites are forbidden
On paper (the original 1890 concordance), on a phone (mobile apps like Blue Letter Bible), and on the full internet (websites like Bible Hub)
mc.why: All three forms contain the same essential content: every Hebrew and Greek word in the Bible keyed to a number, with a brief definition, and a list of every verse where the word appears. Paper for the historic foundation, phone for the daily workman, internet for the deep dive. The number is language-neutral — G25 is G25 in every tool.

mc.stem: Once you know a word's Strong's number, what larger Greek and Hebrew lexicons can you then consult, since they are also keyed to Strong's numbers?
options: Wikipedia and YouTube
The Strong's number unlocks no other resources beyond Strong's own dictionary
Thayer's Greek-English Lexicon (NT) and Brown-Driver-Briggs (OT Hebrew) — both keyed to Strong's, vastly more detailed than Strong's brief entries
Only the most expensive Logos Pro library, costing thousands of dollars
mc.why: Strong's brief entries (usually one or two sentences) are a starting point, not the last word. Thayer's Greek-English Lexicon and Brown-Driver-Briggs (BDB) Hebrew-English Lexicon are vastly more detailed scholarly tools, both keyed to Strong's numbers. Find the Strong's number once, and a whole library of further lexicons opens up. Most are free on Blue Letter Bible and Bible Hub.

mc.stem: What is the difference between a CONCORDANCE and a LEXICON?
options: A concordance lists every verse where an English word appears (and points to the original-language word); a lexicon is a dictionary of the original-language words themselves
A concordance is for Hebrew and a lexicon is for Greek
A concordance is a small book and a lexicon is a large book — the only difference is size
A concordance is online and a lexicon is on paper
mc.why: A concordance is an index from the English (or Spanish) Bible to the original-language word: 'Here is every verse where the word "love" appears in the KJV, and here is the Strong's number for each.' A lexicon is a dictionary of the original-language words themselves: 'Here is what agapaô means, what its tenses are, what its synonyms are.' Strong's volume includes both: the concordance in front, the lexicons in back.

mc.stem: What is the relationship between Wycliffe's English Bible (1380s), Tyndale's English New Testament (1525), and Strong's Concordance (1890)?
options: All three are part of a long democratizing tradition: each chipped away at the wall between the ordinary Christian and the original Word, putting Scripture and its tools into the hand of the common believer
They are completely unrelated works
They are all Roman Catholic productions
Strong's was an attempt to undo what Wycliffe and Tyndale did
mc.why: Wycliffe gave the English peasant the Bible in his own tongue (1380s). Tyndale printed the NT in the language of plowboys (1525) and was martyred for it in 1536. Cruden's concordance in 1737 indexed the English Bible. Strong's 1890 concordance gave the layperson access to the underlying Hebrew and Greek. Each step put more of the Word into more hands. Strong's is the modern hammer in a centuries-long demolition of the seminary wall.

mc.stem: In Unit 9 you learned several Greek words with their Strong's numbers. What are the correct Strong's numbers for pistis, sôzô, dikaiosynê, and kyrios?
options: All four Greek words share the same number G0001
H4102, H4982, H1343, H2962 (with Hebrew H prefixes)
Strong's numbers were never assigned to Greek words
G4102 (pistis), G4982 (sôzô), G1343 (dikaiosynê), G2962 (kyrios)
mc.why: Each Greek word has its own unique Strong's number: pistis G4102 (faith), sôzô G4982 (save), dikaiosynê G1343 (righteousness), kyrios G2962 (Lord). Add Unit 8: logos G3056 (Word), agapê G26 (love), charis G5485 (grace), pneuma G4151 (Spirit). The eight numbers form the New Testament's salvation vocabulary. Memorize none of them; learn instead to look them up in seconds with Strong's tools.

mc.stem: What is the proper six-step workflow for a complete Strong's-based word study, as you will apply it in Unit 11?
options: (1) Read your verse and pick a meaningful word; (2) look up the Strong's number; (3) read the lexicon entry; (4) look up every other occurrence of the same Strong's number; (5) read 5–10 of those verses noting how context shapes meaning; (6) return to your original verse and reread with the word's range in mind
Pray, sing a hymn, recite the creed, take communion, fast for 40 days, then guess at the meaning
Memorize the entire concordance from beginning to end
Email a Greek professor and wait three weeks for him to reply
mc.why: The complete word-study workflow: (1) read your verse and pick a word, (2) find the Strong's number, (3) read the lexicon entry, (4) click 'every occurrence' of the same Strong's number, (5) read several of those verses to see the word in different contexts, (6) return to your original verse and reread with the word's full range now in your mind. The whole process takes about fifteen minutes in Blue Letter Bible. It used to take a seminary degree.

mc.stem: Section III of this unit walked through a live example on biblehub.com using Romans 1:17 and the Greek word dikaiosynê (Strong's G1343). This was the same verse and same Greek word that Martin Luther read in Erasmus's 1516 Greek New Testament. What historic discovery did Luther make, which any modern believer with a phone can now replicate in thirty seconds?
options: That dikaiosynê theou ('the righteousness of God') in Romans 1:17 refers to the righteousness God GIVES to those who believe, not the standard God demands — the 'gates of paradise' insight that ignited the Reformation in 1517
That the apostle Paul never actually visited the city of Rome
That the Greek New Testament had been written by medieval monks
That Romans was originally written in Latin, not Greek
mc.why: Luther's 1516 reading of Romans 1:17 in Erasmus's freshly printed Greek NT revealed that dikaiosynê theou is the righteousness God gives by grace through faith, not the impossible standard He demands. Luther later wrote that he 'felt as if reborn and had gone through open gates into paradise itself.' That single Greek-word insight ignited the Reformation a year later. Five centuries later any believer with biblehub.com or Blue Letter Bible can find G1343, read the same Thayer's entry, and reach the same conclusion in under a minute. The democratization Wycliffe-Tyndale-Cruden-Strong begun is now complete: the discovery that took the German monk twenty years to find takes the Mexican student thirty seconds. That is what Strong's numbers do.
